title: What do you think of this use of LLMs in a mystery game? Every passenger at my border booth is an AI character (free demo)
author: Aromatic-Being5180
selftext:
The Long Season is a co-op mystery game set on Caldera, a sunny tax haven island where nobody who enters ever leaves. You're the border inspector, and there are no dialogue options: you question every passenger in your own words, by voice or by typing, then check their papers, call their hotel, search their bags, and decide who gets in.



Every passenger is played live by a language model. Each one has a written character sheet with who they really are, what they're hiding and how they lie, and the model improvises from it: it answers, dodges, gets nervous, and only cracks when you corner it with real evidence. The same goes for the people you call on the phone and the emails you receive. The model also chooses, line by line, which of the character's drawn facial expressions appears at the booth, so the face reacts to what you say.



For the art, I generate drafts with an image model, then snap them back onto the real pixel grid and clean them up by hand, so everything keeps the same chunky pixel style. The walking characters come from a pixel-art generation tool and get the same hand fixes. AI tools also helped me with the code.



I'm curious what this community thinks: does this feel like a good use of an LLM in a game, or does it get in the way? And how does the art read to you?



The demo is free, in the browser and on Windows: [https://dporto.itch.io/the-long-season](https://dporto.itch.io/the-long-season)

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
I think at the moment it is a horrible idea to try and incorporate LLMs directly into gameplay.

You're asking the user to connect to and pay for an API service just to play a simple indie game. The value proposition is totally crap, IMHO. 

If local models come out that are decent at play and easy enough to incorporate into an engine, that'll be an interesting thing to explore. But just trying to plug your game into a cloud model only turns the game into a - at best - a glorified prompt client (at worst, a bad prompt client).

replies.author: Aromatic-Being5180
replies.body:
Fair point if players had to bring their own API key, I'd hate that too. They don't: there's no key, no account and no payment. The model runs on my server and the demo is free, the cost is on me.

And it's honestly sustainable: with a small fast model, short prompts, prompt caching and short replies, a whole session costs very little, so I can keep it free.

On the "prompt client" part: the LLM only plays the characters. The game around it is regular game design: documents to check, a phone and a computer to verify stories, evidence you can show, bribes, verdicts with consequences, a story about the island. The game tracks what's true and what you can prove, not the model.

Local models are on my radar too, once they can stay in character and lie consistently on normal hardware. If you try it for five minutes I'd honestly like to hear if it still feels like a prompt client.

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
This is a great fit for an LLM, because the core verb is talking. The player has a built-in reason to type something, which is the hardest part to get right.

The bit I'd watch is "only cracks when you corner it with real evidence." If cracking is the model's judgement call, a clever or pushy player can talk a character into confessing without the evidence. A sturdier pattern is letting the game own that state. A passenger only becomes "crackable" once a flag like papers_mismatch or hotel_denied is set, and the model is told whether it may break or must hold.

I'm the dev of Hatched, a browser city where every resident is an AI and you're the voice in one citizen's head, and my biggest surprise was how few players talked at all. Most just watched until I put the chat front and center. A border booth solves that by design, which I'm a bit jealous of. The face picking per line is a lovely touch too.

replies.author: Aromatic-Being5180
replies.body:
Thanks, great point. The server already makes them crack first and only admit on a later turn, but when they crack is still the model's call. Gating it on flags like papers\_mismatch is a smart fix, I'll try it.

Funny about Hatched, here the booth forces the talking. Glad you liked the faces!

replies.author: aura-32
replies.body: Crack first, admit later is a nice touch, it gives the player that moment of "I've got you" before the confession. Hope the flags work out. Good luck with the demo!

replies.author: dicehandz
replies.body: im curious how this works though, are those calls to the LLM coming from your tokens?  wouldnt this blast through your budget?

replies.author: Aromatic-Being5180
replies.body:
Yes, they're on my tokens. It doesn't blast through it though: a full half-hour session costs one to two cents, and this whole week of players cost me about half a dollar. A small fast model, short replies and prompt caching keep it that cheap.

And it's capped, of course: the key never leaves the server, every player has a limit per minute and per day, replies have a max length, and passengers get tired and leave if you keep them at the booth too long.

The design keeps it bounded too. Like in Disco Elysium, every question will move the clock forward, so a day at the booth has a natural end and pushing too much leads toward a game over, not an endless chat.

If it grows, say on Steam, at that scale it gets cheaper to run an open model on our own efficient GPUs than to pay per call. And for someone who wants to play forever, there's always the option of running a smaller model locally on their own GPU.

replies.author: Aromatic-Being5180
replies.body: And worst case, if it ever ran as a free game at scale, a single ad per session like in mobile games would already cover the API cost. A half-hour session costs one to two cents, which is less than what one ad usually pays.

replies.author: aura-32
replies.body: It would if every citizen called a paid model all the time, so they don't. By default every citizen in Hatched runs on a free local rules brain, which costs nothing to run. Players who want real conversations can plug in their own key (Anthropic, OpenRouter or any OpenAI-compatible API), and new players get 40 free thoughts on free OpenRouter models to feel the difference. Even with a model connected, it's only called for moments that matter, like a job offer, a fight or a conversation, and cheap rules handle the routine. That routing cut model costs about 10x.

comments.author: ComputerTraining9274
comments.body:
I’ve played around doing this some with local models to voice AI dialogue and have like a “social deduction” style game where you try to outsmart the AIs but using in game lore and events.

Unfortunately right now I just don’t think it’s really feasible just due to hardware limitations, obviously running on a remote server like you’re doing allows for running better models, but even then the compute costs and network latency just make the gameplay slow and not really fun.

Local models were even worse too, you need a super high end graphics card to get even decent results and trying to optimize with quantized models just doesn’t cut it.

It’s a cool idea and definitely something that will become more and more viable as hardware catches up, but right now I’d just build it with the understanding that it’s realistically going to be a tech demo instead of an actually playable game

replies.author: Aromatic-Being5180
replies.body: Agree on local models, they're not there yet for characters who have to lie consistently. But calling a small fast model through an API has worked better than I expected. Replies come back in about two seconds, which at a border booth just feels like the passenger thinking. And it's cheap: a full half-hour session costs one to two cents in API calls, so I can keep the demo free. Curious what latency you were seeing with your setup?

replies.author: ComputerTraining9274
replies.body:
Latency I was experiencing was all local and mostly just inference models running slow trying to compare user inputs and run that against text game rules and character history and archetypes

Cool to hear you’ve found a good use case and from the costs you’ve mentioned that’s certainly negligible! Good luck with the project!

comments.author: Aware-Soil-8031
comments.body:
Para programar evidentemente es una gran ayuda, pero evitaría usar imágenes generadas con IA, son muy evidentes para cualquiera y provocan bastante rechazo para la mayoría. Creo que prefiero un arte regulero de un humano con personalidad, que un muy buen arte de IA genérico.  
Intenta rehacer los gráficos a mano, a ver como queda.

replies.author: Aromatic-Being5180
replies.body: I’ve been trying an approach where I first generate images using AI, then reduce their resolution, and finally refine and edit them manually. However, if you’re saying it’s too noticeable, I’ll try a different method I’m an engineer, not an artist, unfortunately

comments.author: JorgitoEstrella
comments.body: This is an excellent idea but I think is limited by our tech rn like the devs of the game "teaching your sister how to drive" that also uses an llm lost thousands of dollars just by having a demo.

replies.author: Aromatic-Being5180
replies.body: That story is a good warning, but the setup is quite different here. It's story-driven: each day at the booth ends, the game has an end, it's not an open loop where you can talk forever, and the in-game clock keeps sessions bounded. The passengers answer in text, they don't speak, and if you use the mic a small model just transcribes it. So it's about 5–6 cents per hour of play. If it went viral it would still cost real money, so there are per-player limits and I'd cap the daily spend, but at a cent or two per player it's cheaper than any ad.
